lines.text: Shells and silver, paper and gold, banks, bubbles and crashes. This is the story of money and the economy, from Babylon's laws to Bitcoin.
Almost four thousand years ago, the king of Babylon carved his laws on a stone pillar, with rules for trade, wages and loans for all to see.
Long before coins, people paid with shells. Cowries were small, hard to forge and easy to count, and they served as money across three continents.
In the kingdom of Lydia, King Croesus struck coins of gold and of silver in fixed weights, spreading the idea of money stamped by the state.
In China, the Qin dynasty standardised a round bronze coin with a square hole. Strung in bundles, it served for over two thousand years.
Rome paid its soldiers in silver denarii. But as emperors needed ever more for their armies, the silver in each coin shrank.
Meanwhile the Silk Road linked China with India, Persia and the Mediterranean, carrying silk, spices, ideas and even the plague.
In 696 the caliph Abd al-Malik issued a gold dinar with Arabic writing in place of pictures. Several countries still call their money the dinar.
In England, silver pennies gave rise to the pound sterling, one of the oldest currencies still in use, and once the money of world trade.
Around the year one thousand, China began to use paper money, first from merchants, then from the state. Europe would not catch up for centuries.
In northern Europe, the towns of the Hanseatic League banded together around the Baltic and North Seas to protect their trade, from London to Novgorod.
Florence struck its gold florin in the thirteenth century, and its steady quality made it a standard of trade across Europe.
Venice answered with the ducat, prized across the Mediterranean for its purity and copied by many other states.
In 1397 Giovanni de Medici founded a bank with branches across Europe. Its wealth let his family rule Florence and pay for Renaissance art.
Then, after 1492, plants, animals, people and diseases crossed the Atlantic both ways, and the world's economy was remade.
From the silver mines of Spanish America came the Spanish dollar, a world currency. The dollar sign itself comes from it.
And for several centuries, European merchants shipped millions of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to work plantations and mines, a trade that shaped three continents.
With more people and a flood of American silver, prices in Europe rose for a century and a half, favouring merchants and landowners over wage earners.
In 1600 Elizabeth the First chartered the East India Company. It traded tea, cotton and spices, and grew into the ruler of much of India.
Two years later the Dutch East India Company sold shares to the public, and is often called the first modern corporation.
To trade those shares, Amsterdam set up the first modern stock exchange.
In the 1630s the Dutch went wild for tulip bulbs. Prices soared, then collapsed, the best known early bubble, though its size is debated.
In 1694 the Bank of England was founded in London to lend to the government. It is still Britain's central bank.
The South Sea Company took over part of Britain's debt. In 1720 its shares soared and crashed, ruining many investors.
In Scotland, Adam Smith argued that trade, specialised work and competition could make whole nations richer.
Meanwhile Britain was turning from hand work to machines and factories, with steam power, railways and big cities.
The economist David Ricardo showed that two countries gain from trade even when one makes everything better, the idea of comparative advantage.
In 1776 Smith published The Wealth of Nations, seen as the founding book of modern economics.
In 1792 traders met under a buttonwood tree on Wall Street, the start of what became the world's largest stock exchange.
That same year the Coinage Act set up the United States dollar, which after the Second World War would become the world's main reserve currency.
Karl Marx, born in Germany in 1818, argued that history is driven by struggles between classes, and his writing would shape politics worldwide.
In 1821 Britain tied the pound to a fixed amount of gold. Many nations followed, and the gold standard held for a century and a half.
Gold was found at Sutter's Mill in 1848, and hundreds of thousands rushed to California. San Francisco boomed, and Native peoples paid the price.
In 1867 Marx published Das Kapital, his attack on capitalism, which would inspire communist movements and governments.
Keynes, the British economist, would later argue that in a slump governments should spend more to bring back demand and jobs.
Friedrich Hayek replied that free markets use knowledge better than any planner, and became a hero of free-market reformers.
In 1907 a run on New York banks sent shares tumbling, and J. P. Morgan organised a rescue. It was a warning.
Milton Friedman, born in 1912, would argue that inflation comes from printing too much money, and champion free markets.
After that panic, the United States founded its central bank, the Federal Reserve, in 1913.
After the First World War, German money became almost worthless. People carried banknotes in wheelbarrows, and savings vanished.
In 1928 Stalin launched five-year plans for the whole Soviet economy, building heavy industry at great speed and terrible human cost.
Then, in October 1929, prices on Wall Street plunged over several days, after years of rises.
The Great Depression followed, the deepest downturn of the century. Millions around the world lost their jobs and homes.
In America, Franklin Roosevelt answered with the New Deal: public works, relief and reform of the banks.
In 1944, at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire, the Allies tied the world's currencies to the dollar, and the dollar to gold.
From those talks came the International Monetary Fund, which lends to governments in trouble and watches the world economy.
And the World Bank, first to rebuild Europe, and now to lend to poorer countries for roads, schools and power.
In 1948 the Marshall Plan sent billions of American dollars to rebuild western Europe after the war.
In 1950 the Diners Club card let people buy now and pay later, and credit cards soon spread through shops worldwide.
Six European countries opened a common market, the European Economic Community, which grew into the European Union.
In 1960 five oil-producing states met in Baghdad and founded OPEC, whose decisions can move world oil prices.
And in 1967 Barclays installed the first cash machine in London, money at any hour.
In 1971 the United States stopped exchanging dollars for gold. Bretton Woods broke, and currencies began to float.
Two years later Arab producers cut oil supplies. Fuel queues and soaring prices followed, and the world learned to save energy.
In 1978 China, under Deng Xiaoping, let farmers and firms sell for profit and opened to foreign investment, starting decades of fast growth.
In Japan, land and share prices climbed to extraordinary heights in the late eighties, then fell, leaving a lost decade.
On Black Monday in October 1987, markets around the world plunged, the Dow's largest one-day fall, though the economy recovered faster than feared.
In 1995 the World Trade Organization took over setting the rules of trade between nations, from its seat in Geneva.
Meanwhile internet shares soared, even for firms with no profits, until the bubble burst in 2000.
In 1997 Thailand's currency collapsed, and the crisis spread across East Asia. Indonesia, South Korea and Thailand needed rescue loans.
In 1999 the euro was born, and within three years its notes and coins replaced the franc, the mark and many more.
That year PayPal let people pay online with just an email address, the first widely used online wallet.
In Zimbabwe, prices at the peak doubled in days. The money became worthless, and people turned to the American dollar.
In Kenya, M-Pesa let people send money by text message, giving millions a way to pay and save without a bank.
Then American house prices fell, bad mortgages spread, and Lehman Brothers failed. Governments spent vast sums to save the banks.
In the aftermath came Bitcoin, money with no bank in the middle, tracked in a shared public record.
In 2010 Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus struggled with their debts. Rescues came with cuts, and the euro's future was in question.
In 2016 India launched UPI, instant payments from a phone, now used billions of times a month.
From 2018 the United States and China put tariffs on each other's goods, a trade war between the two largest economies.
In 2020 the pandemic shut down much of the world, and the economy fell faster than at any time since the Great Depression.
After it, and after Russia invaded Ukraine, prices surged, the highest inflation in forty years in many countries.
And in 2025 the United States put sweeping tariffs on imports from almost every country, the highest in a century.
From cowrie shells to phones that pay, money keeps changing shape, and so does the world it moves.
